content: Ensuring the safety of children is a critical priority. In Naivasha, Kenya, local authorities have implemented several measures to enhance safety around schools. These measures include constructing pedestrian crossings, dedicated foot and cycle paths, and speed humps. They have also reduced speed limits to 30 km/h and enforced these limits rigorously. Improved street lighting has been installed to increase visibility, and children are encouraged to use reflective backpacks to enhance their visibility. Additionally, crossing guards are provided to ensure proper supervision. School safety zones have been introduced, incorporating a range of speed reduction measures, car-free zones, safe drop-off and pick-up points, and crossing guards. Signalized intersections near schools have been adjusted to allow for longer crossing times. Designated play areas for children have been established away from roads, and investments have been made in safe public transportation systems. Vehicle design adaptations play a significant role in protecting children both inside and outside vehicles, including those on bicycles and motorcycles. Specific vehicle safety measures for children include the mandatory installation of energy-absorbing crumple zones to protect passengers during crashes, redesigning vehicle fronts to be more pedestrian-friendly, equipping vehicles with cameras and audible alarms to detect small objects not visible in rear-view mirrors, and installing alcohol interlock systems in vehicles of individuals convicted of drinking and driving. Young, novice drivers, particularly those as young as 15 years old in some countries, contribute significantly to road traffic crashes due to factors such as speeding, driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, and texting while driving. Graduated driver licensing programs, which impose restrictions and follow a phased approach, have been shown to reduce road traffic crashes and fatalities among this group by as much as 46%. These programs include strategies such as lowering blood alcohol concentration (BAC) limits for young or novice drivers, requiring supervised driving with a responsible adult for a designated period, restricting nighttime driving and driving with passengers, and enforcing zero tolerance for traffic offenses, including texting while driving. In Queensland, Australia, the graduated driver licensing program was enhanced in 2007 to extend the learner period from six to twelve months, increase supervised driving hours to 100 hours (including 10 hours of nighttime driving), and prohibit mobile phone use to address distracted driving. Driving hours must be logged and certified before taking the practical driving test. These measures have significantly reduced road traffic crashes among young drivers. Providing appropriate care for injured children is essential. Strengthening emergency care and rehabilitation services is the best approach to improving outcomes for all road traffic victims, with special considerations for children. Key strategies include educating caregivers and teachers on immediate stabilization of injuries and establishing plans for transporting injured children to care facilities. Prehospital and facility-based providers should be trained in the physiological differences between children and adults and the distinct treatment needs of children. Emergency vehicles should be equipped with child-sized medical equipment and supplies. Hospitals should be made as child-friendly as possible to minimize additional trauma, and pediatric-specific rehabilitation services, including home-based rehabilitation and access to community-based centers, should be improved. Counseling services should be made available to address the psychological impact of road traffic injuries on children and their families, as well as practical considerations such as legislative and financial queries. Supervising children around roads is crucial, as young children have limited capacity to evaluate risks. Parents and caregivers play a vital role in helping children interpret their surroundings and ensuring their safety in complex road environments. Supervision complements other interventions, such as ensuring children use helmets, car seats, and seat belts, and adhere to school safety zone protocols. Combined with other strategies, supervision can significantly reduce the likelihood of children being involved in road traffic crashes. Road traffic deaths and injuries are preventable. Countries that have demonstrated the political will to address this issue have saved the lives of hundreds of thousands of children and conserved substantial national resources. The strategies outlined in this document are among the most effective for keeping children safe on the road. If implemented globally, they could contribute significantly to achieving the Decade of Action for Road Safety 2011–2020 goal of saving five million lives.
